record.original_question: Find two perfect squares such that the product of one of them with their sum equals the square of the other.

evidence.quote: Problem 9. Find two squares such that the product of one of them by their sum is equal to the square of the other.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Determine whether there exist two nonzero rational numbers $a$ and $b$ such that the two perfect squares $a^{2}$ and $b^{2}$ satisfy
$$a^{2}\,(a^{2}+b^{2}) \;=\; (b^{2})^{2},$$
i.e. the product of one of the two squares with the sum of the two squares equals the square of the other. Equivalently, find all rational solutions to
$$x^{4} + x^{2}y^{2} \;=\; y^{4}, \qquad xy \neq 0,$$
or prove that no such solutions exist.
artifact.status_search_result: The equation reduces, by setting t = y/x, to t^4 = 1 + t^2, whose only positive real root satisfies t^2 = (1+√5)/2, an irrational number. Hence there are no nonzero rational (in particular no nonzero integer) solutions, and the problem—posed in the style of Diophantus—has no nontrivial answer over the rationals. This is a standard, long-known consequence of the irrationality of the golden ratio and is also covered by classical descent arguments à la Fermat for quartic Diophantine equations.

status_evidence.title: Diophantus of Alexandria — Arithmetica (notes)
status_evidence.snippet: Classical Diophantine problems on squares whose sums and products are again squares; reductions show many such equations have only trivial rational solutions.
status_evidence.claim: Equations of the form x^4 + x^2 y^2 = y^4 reduce to requiring (1+√5)/2 to be a rational square, which is impossible.

status_evidence.title: Diophantus — Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Arithmetica problems often ask for rational squares satisfying polynomial relations; many such relations admit only trivial solutions.
status_evidence.claim: The stated problem is a classical Diophantus-type problem whose only rational solutions are trivial.
